set.detail:
The First Illyrian War (229-228) was Rome's first military intervention east of the Adriatic. The Ardiaean kingdom under Agron and, after his death in 231, his widow Teuta, regent for Pinnes, had expanded along the Adriatic coast, taking Phoenice in Epirus (230) and raiding the Greek west with fleets of light lembi. Illyrian pirates had attacked Italian traders, many of them from Brundisium and other southern towns. In 230 Rome sent the brothers Gaius and Lucius Coruncanius to Teuta; according to Polybius, she replied that Illyrian royal custom did not restrain private piracy, and one envoy (Appian says the Issaean Cleemporus was also killed) was murdered on the way home.

In 229 the Illyrians defeated the Achaean and Aetolian fleets off Paxos, took Corcyra and besieged Epidamnus and Issa. Rome sent both consuls: Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus with 200 ships and Lucius Postumius Albinus with 20,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry. Demetrius of Pharos, Teuta's governor at Corcyra, surrendered the island; Rome relieved Epidamnus and Issa, received the submission of the Parthini and Atintani, and forced Teuta to flee to Rhizon. In spring 228 she made peace, paying tribute, giving up most of Illyria and agreeing not to sail south of Lissus with more than two unarmed ships.

Rome created a protectorate of free communities (Corcyra, Apollonia, Epidamnus, Issa, the Parthini and Atintani) without annexing territory, and sent envoys to the Aetolian and Achaean Leagues, Corinth and Athens to explain its action; Corinth admitted Romans to the Isthmian Games. Polybius (2.2-12) regarded the war as the first Roman contact with Greece and the beginning of Roman involvement in Greek affairs. Historians debate its motives: Holleaux emphasised commercial pressure from Italian traders and the defence of the Adriatic; Harris and Derow see a broader Roman aggressiveness; Eckstein sees Rome responding to Illyrian expansion in a multipolar system. The settlement, which elevated Demetrius of Pharos, led to the Second Illyrian War ten years later and contributed to friction with Macedon.

scholarship: Holleaux, Rome, la Grèce et les monarchies hellénistiques (1921)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
Wilkes, The Illyrians (1992)

set.detail:
The Second Illyrian War (219) was directed against Demetrius of Pharos, the Greek adventurer whom Rome had installed as a dynast in Illyria in 228 as reward for surrendering Corcyra. Demetrius married Triteuta, mother of the young king Pinnes, became guardian of the Ardiaean kingdom, and allied with Antigonus Doson, fighting at Sellasia (222). Encouraged by Rome's preoccupation with the Gauls and the growing tension with Carthage, he broke the treaty of 228 by sailing south of Lissus with 90 lembi in 220, attacking Pylos and raiding the Cyclades with Scerdilaidas, and by attacking cities in the Roman protectorate.

In 219 Rome sent both consuls, Lucius Aemilius Paullus (later killed at Cannae) and Marcus Livius Salinator. They stormed Dimale, Demetrius' strongest fortress, in seven days, which led other towns to surrender. Demetrius had prepared to defend Pharos with his best troops. Paullus landed his main force by night in a hidden bay, and at dawn sent 20 ships to attack the harbour openly; when Demetrius led his men out against them, the main Roman force cut him off from the city. Demetrius escaped by boat to Philip V of Macedon, where he became an influential adviser, urging Philip to take advantage of Rome's war with Hannibal. Pharos was razed.

The war was brief and successful, and both consuls celebrated triumphs; Livius Salinator was later convicted of unfair division of the booty. Polybius (3.16-19) insists that Rome fought it just before the war with Hannibal, believing that it had time to settle Illyrian affairs first, which explains the delay in aiding Saguntum. The war strengthened Roman control of the Adriatic coast, but Demetrius' flight to Philip and his influence there helped bring Macedon into alliance with Hannibal in 215 and led to the First Macedonian War. Demetrius was killed in 214 attacking Messene. The protectorate's existence would be a recurring cause of Roman friction with Macedon.

scholarship: Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
Wilkes, The Illyrians (1992)

set.detail:
The Third Illyrian War (168) was a short campaign against Genthius, king of the Illyrians at Scodra, who had joined Perseus during the Third Macedonian War. Genthius, son of Pleuratus, had been a nominal friend of Rome; Roman envoys had complained of Illyrian piracy against Italian merchants. Perseus' envoys, including Pleuratus the Illyrian exile, negotiated an alliance in 169/168, promising a subsidy of 300 talents. Perseus paid only ten talents, keeping the rest when Genthius had committed himself by imprisoning two Roman envoys, a breach of the law of nations. Polybius and Livy present Perseus' meanness as a major cause of his downfall.

In 168 the praetor Lucius Anicius Gallus crossed from Brundisium with two legions, defeated Genthius' fleet of lembi, and marched on Scodra. Genthius, with 15,000 men, offered battle but was quickly defeated and fled into the city; after asking for a three-day truce, he surrendered with his family. The war lasted 30 days, as Livy notes (44.32). Anicius then took the rest of Illyria and joined Aemilius Paullus in Epirus.

The Illyrian kingdom was abolished. Like Macedonia, Illyria was declared free and divided into three parts, which paid half their former tribute to Rome, except the communities that had sided with Rome early (the Issaeans, Taulantii, Pirustae of the Daorsi, the Dassaretii and the people of Rhizon and Olcinium), which were exempted. Anicius celebrated a triumph in 167, parading Genthius and his family; at the victory games he made Greek musicians fight on stage, an episode Polybius (30.22) describes with disdain. Genthius was imprisoned at Spoletium and then Iguvium. The war completed the Roman settlement of the Adriatic coast, although the Dalmatians and other peoples further north remained independent and troublesome, leading to the Dalmatian War of 156-155. Coins of Genthius from Scodra, with his portrait and a lembus, survive.

scholarship: Wilkes, The Illyrians (1992)
Dzino, Illyricum in Roman Politics 229 BC-AD 68 (2010)

set.detail:
The Gallic War of 225-222 was the decisive struggle between Rome and the Celts of the Po valley. Its background was the Roman settlement of the ager Gallicus south of Ariminum under the Lex Flaminia (232), which the Boii and Insubres saw as a threat to their own land. In 225 they hired Gaesatae, professional warriors from beyond the Alps, under the kings Concolitanus and Aneroestes, and invaded Etruria with, Polybius says, 50,000 infantry and 20,000 cavalry and chariots. Rome mobilised its whole alliance (the census of 225, preserved by Polybius, recorded 700,000 infantry and 70,000 cavalry available) and used ritual means: a Gallic and a Greek couple were buried alive in the Forum Boarium in 228.

The Gauls defeated a praetor near Faesulae and reached Clusium, but withdrew when the consul Papus approached, and were caught between two consular armies at Telamon, where 40,000 were killed. In 224 the consuls Fulvius Flaccus and Manlius Torquatus invaded the Boian country, forcing the Boii to submit. In 223 Gaius Flaminius and Publius Furius crossed the Po into Insubrian territory; disregarding a Senate order to return, Flaminius won a battle near the Adda, using the triarii's thrusting spears in the front line against Gallic swords. In 222 the Insubres asked for peace but were refused; they hired 30,000 Gaesatae. Marcus Claudius Marcellus killed King Viridomarus at Clastidium and won the spolia opima, while Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio took Acerrae and Mediolanum; the Insubres surrendered.

Rome followed the victory by building the Via Flaminia to Ariminum (220) and by founding the Latin colonies of Placentia and Cremona (218) on the Po. But the conquest was incomplete: when Hannibal arrived in 218, the Boii and Insubres rose again, and the region was only pacified between 200 and 191. Polybius (2.14-35) provides a detailed account, emphasising the Celtic way of war and Roman resilience, derived from Fabius Pictor, a participant. The war marked the end of the 'Gallic terror' that had haunted Rome since the sack of 390 and the beginning of Roman Cisalpine Gaul.

scholarship: Williams, Beyond the Rubicon: Romans and Gauls in Republican Italy (2001)
Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957)

set.detail:
The Gallic War of 200-191 completed the Roman conquest of Cisalpine Gaul after the Second Punic War, during which the Boii and Insubres had supported Hannibal and Mago. In 200 a coalition of Insubres, Boii and Cenomani, led by a Carthaginian officer named Hamilcar who had remained in Italy, sacked the Latin colony of Placentia and besieged Cremona; the praetor Lucius Furius Purpurio defeated them, killing (in one version) Hamilcar and 35,000 Gauls. The fighting continued annually with mixed results: in 199 the praetor Gnaeus Baebius Tamphilus was defeated by the Insubres; in 197 Gaius Cornelius Cethegus detached the Cenomani from the Insubres and won at the Mincius, while Quintus Minucius Rufus campaigned against the Boii and Ligurians.

In 196 Marcus Claudius Marcellus, after an ambush by the Boii, defeated the Insubres and took Comum; in 195 Lucius Valerius Flaccus defeated the Boii near the Litana forest and rebuilt Placentia and Cremona. In 194 and 193 the Boii resisted fiercely: Tiberius Sempronius Longus fought an indecisive battle near Mutina (194); in 193 Lucius Cornelius Merula won a costly victory near Mutina, claiming 14,000 Gauls killed. In 191 Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica defeated the Boii decisively, confiscated half their territory, and celebrated a triumph, displaying 1,471 gold torques. Livy says few Boii were left, though they survived as a people; later tradition that they migrated across the Alps to Bohemia (Boiohaemum) is disputed.

The conquest was followed by an intense programme of colonisation and road building: the Latin colony of Bononia (189), Placentia and Cremona reinforced (190), the Via Aemilia (187), the citizen colonies of Parma and Mutina (183), the Latin colony of Aquileia (181). Within a generation the region south of the Po became thoroughly Romanised, and Latin replaced Celtic. Polybius (2.35) says the Gauls were driven from the Po plain except for a few communities in the Alpine foothills. Livy's books 31-36 are the main source, with numerous annalistic exaggerations of casualty figures. The Insubres and Cenomani, north of the Po, were treated as allies and kept their land.

scholarship: Williams, Beyond the Rubicon (2001)
Toynbee, Hannibal's Legacy II (1965)

set.detail:
The Istrian Wars (221 and 178-177) were Rome's campaigns against the Histri, an Illyrian or Venetic people of the Istrian peninsula at the head of the Adriatic. In 221 the consuls Publius Cornelius Scipio Asina and Marcus Minucius Rufus subdued the Histri, accused of piracy against Roman grain ships; the campaign is known only from brief notices in Eutropius, Orosius and Zonaras, and is often called the First Istrian War.

The Second Istrian War arose from the foundation of the Latin colony of Aquileia (181), which the Histri saw as a threat. In 178 the consul Aulus Manlius Vulso invaded Istria without senatorial authorisation; his camp near the Timavus (Timavo) was surprised by the Histri under King Aepulo and captured, and the Roman soldiers fled to the ships. Livy says the Istrians, who had found the camp full of wine and food, were so drunk when the Romans counterattacked that they were cut down in their sleep, 8,000 killed. The war continued in 177 with the consul Gaius Claudius Pulcher, who besieged the Istrian stronghold of Nesactium; the Romans diverted the river that supplied the town, and the defenders killed their wives and children and threw their bodies from the walls before the city fell. Aepulo killed himself. Mutila and Faveria were taken; 5,632 captives were sold.

Claudius celebrated a triumph over the Histri and Ligurians in 177. Istria was nominally subject to Rome but remained restless; further campaigns followed in 129 (Gaius Sempronius Tuditanus, who triumphed) and later, and the region was only fully integrated under Augustus, who included it in Italy (regio X). Livy (41.1-11) is the main source for the war of 178-177, which shows the problems of discipline and command in Roman armies of the period. Excavations at Nesactium (near Pula) have revealed the Histrian stronghold and its sanctuary, with sculptures showing Hellenistic influence.

scholarship: Wilkes, The Illyrians (1992)
Dzino, Illyricum in Roman Politics (2010)

set.detail:
The Ligurian Wars (238-155) were a long series of campaigns against the Ligurian peoples of the northern Apennines and the coastal mountains between the Arno and the Rhône, including the Apuani, Friniates, Ingauni, Intemelii, Statellates and others. The Ligurians lived in fortified hill villages in rugged, forested terrain, practised a mixed economy of pastoralism, farming and raiding, and fought as light infantry in ambushes. Livy (39.1) says Liguria was a training ground for Roman soldiers, where there was nothing to plunder but much fighting.

The first campaigns (238-233) protected Pisae and the coastal route; Quintus Fabius Maximus triumphed in 233. During the Hannibalic war the Ligurians supported Hannibal and Mago (205-203). From 197 to 155 consuls campaigned in Liguria almost every year: Quintus Minucius Thermus fought from Pisae (193-190); Lepidus and Flaminius subdued the Friniates (187); Quintus Marcius Philippus was ambushed in the Saltus Marcius (186), losing 4,000 men; Aemilius Paullus defeated the Ingauni (181); and in 180 the proconsuls Cornelius Cethegus and Baebius Tamphilus deported 40,000 Apuan men with their families to Samnium (the Ligures Baebiani and Corneliani, known from the bronze alimentary tablet of Trajan). The Ligurians took Mutina in 177 and killed the consul Petillius in 176. In 173 the consul Marcus Popillius Laenas attacked the Statellates, who had not fought Rome, and enslaved them, provoking a scandal in the Senate.

Colonies secured the conquest: Luna (177), Luca (180 or 177), and the Via Aemilia and Via Postumia (148). In 154 Quintus Opimius campaigned against the Oxybii and Deciates near Massalia, Rome's first operation beyond the Alps. The wars produced over a dozen triumphs and much criticism of the brutality of Roman commanders. The Ligurian Wars are a classic example of the Roman 'frontier wars' of attrition, where the aim was security of communications rather than plunder. Livy's books 39-45 are the main source, with many annalistic exaggerations.

scholarship: Toynbee, Hannibal's Legacy II (1965)
Dyson, The Creation of the Roman Frontier (1985)
Harris, Rome in Etruria and Umbria (1971)

set.detail:
The Social War, or War of the Allies (220-217), was fought by the Hellenic alliance (symmachy) founded by Antigonus Doson in 224, led by the young Philip V and including the Achaean League, Boeotia, Phocis, Epirus and Acarnania, against the Aetolian League, joined by Elis and Sparta. Its causes were Aetolian raids on Messenia and the Peloponnese led by Dorimachus and Scopas, culminating in the Aetolian victory over Aratus at Caphyae (220). The alliance declared war at Corinth in 220.

Philip, aged 17 to 20, campaigned brilliantly: in 219 he took towns in Aetolia and Acarnania and in winter 219/8 made a rapid campaign through the Peloponnese, taking Psophis and Lasion and ravaging Elis and Triphylia. In 218 he invaded Aetolia and sacked the federal sanctuary at Thermum, destroying statues and buildings in retaliation for the Aetolian destruction of Dium and Dodona. He also faced intrigues at his court: his minister Apelles and his officers Leontius and Megaleas plotted against him and Aratus, and were executed or committed suicide. Polybius (4-5), who used Aratus' memoirs, gives a detailed account and praises the young Philip as the 'darling of Greece'.

In 217, when news of Trasimene arrived, Philip, on the advice of Demetrius of Pharos, made peace at Naupactus on the basis of the status quo, to turn his attention west. Polybius uses the speech of the Aetolian Agelaus, warning of the 'cloud in the west', to mark the beginning of the interconnection of Greek and Italian affairs. The Social War is important as a demonstration of Macedonian hegemony in Greece before Roman intervention and as the formative experience of Philip V. It also left deep hostility between Philip and the Aetolians, who in 211 allied with Rome. Polybius' account of the war is the most detailed surviving narrative of Hellenistic Greek warfare between Leagues.

scholarship: Walbank, Philip V of Macedon (1940)
Scholten, The Politics of Plunder: Aitolians and their Koinon (2000)

set.detail:
The Fourth Syrian War (219-217) was fought between Antiochus III and Ptolemy IV for control of Coele-Syria (southern Syria, Phoenicia and Palestine), held by the Ptolemies since 301 but claimed by the Seleucids. Antiochus, having defeated the rebel satrap Molon (220), opened the war in 219 by recapturing Seleucia in Pieria, the port of Antioch held by the Ptolemies since the Third Syrian War, and then won over the Ptolemaic general Theodotus the Aetolian, who handed him Tyre and Ptolemais. He occupied much of Phoenicia and Palestine, wintering at Ptolemais.

Ptolemy's ministers Sosibius and Agathocles used negotiations to gain time while they hired mercenaries and trained a new army, including, for the first time, 20,000 native Egyptians in a Macedonian-style phalanx. In 217 Antiochus advanced south with 62,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and 102 Indian elephants, and met Ptolemy, with 70,000 infantry, 5,000 cavalry and 73 African elephants, at Raphia near Gaza on 22 June. Antiochus won on his right, but pursued too far; the Ptolemaic phalanx won in the centre and Antiochus was defeated. He made peace, giving up Coele-Syria except Seleucia in Pieria.

The war is documented in detail by Polybius (5.40-87) and by the trilingual Raphia decree of the Egyptian priests. Its long-term consequences were significant: Antiochus turned to the reconquest of Asia Minor from Achaeus and the eastern satrapies, returning with greater power; the arming of the Egyptians contributed to the native revolts of the following decades, especially the great Theban revolt (205-186). Polybius saw Raphia as contemporaneous with Trasimene and Naupactus, marking the beginning of the interconnection of world history. The Ptolemaic kingdom, though victorious, entered a period of weakness under Ptolemy IV, whose court Polybius portrayed as decadent.

scholarship: Grainger, The Syrian Wars (2010)
Bar-Kochva, The Seleucid Army (1976)
Huss, Untersuchungen zur Aussenpolitik Ptolemaios IV (1976)

set.detail:
The Fifth Syrian War (202-195) was the decisive Seleucid conquest of Coele-Syria from the Ptolemies. When Ptolemy IV died in 204 (his death concealed for a time) and was succeeded by the child Ptolemy V, the Alexandrian court fell into chaos: the ministers Agathocles and Sosibius had Queen Arsinoe III killed, and Agathocles was lynched by the Alexandrian crowd in 203. Antiochus III and Philip V allegedly made a secret pact (203/2) to divide the Ptolemaic overseas possessions, Antiochus taking Coele-Syria and Cyprus, Philip the Aegean and Cyrene.

In 202 Antiochus invaded Coele-Syria, besieged and took Gaza (201), and occupied the region. The Ptolemaic general Scopas, an Aetolian mercenary, counterattacked in 201/200, recovering Judaea and southern Syria. In 200 Antiochus defeated Scopas decisively at Panium (near the source of the Jordan, later Caesarea Philippi); Scopas fled to Sidon, where he was besieged and surrendered in 199/8. Antiochus then occupied all of Coele-Syria and Judaea, where Jerusalem welcomed him; Josephus preserves a decree in which Antiochus granted privileges to the Jews and the temple. He then turned to Asia Minor and the Thracian coast, seizing Ptolemaic possessions in Cilicia, Lycia and Caria, and in 196 crossed to Thrace.

The war ended with a peace in 195 sealed by the marriage of Antiochus' daughter Cleopatra I to Ptolemy V (194/3). Coele-Syria remained Seleucid until the collapse of the dynasty, and the Ptolemaic claims to it led to the Sixth Syrian War (170-168). Rome's involvement was diplomatic: Ptolemaic envoys appealed for help, and the Senate sent an embassy (200) demanding that Antiochus respect Ptolemaic possessions; the fear of a combined Seleucid-Macedonian bloc was one factor in Roman intervention against Philip V. The war's sources include Polybius (books 15-16, fragmentary), Josephus, Jerome's commentary on Daniel (using Porphyry), and the Book of Daniel (11.13-17).

scholarship: Grainger, The Syrian Wars (2010)
Ma, Antiochos III and the Cities of Western Asia Minor (1999)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)

set.detail:
The Sixth Syrian War (170-168) was the last of the wars between the Seleucids and the Ptolemies for Coele-Syria and ended with Roman intervention. In 170 the regents of the young Ptolemy VI, the eunuch Eulaeus and the Syrian Lenaeus, prepared to reconquer Coele-Syria, claiming it as the dowry of Cleopatra I. Antiochus IV struck first: he defeated the Ptolemaic army between Mount Casius and Pelusium, took Pelusium, and occupied much of Egypt. Ptolemy VI fell into his hands, and Antiochus claimed to act as his guardian. The Alexandrians proclaimed Ptolemy VI's younger brother Ptolemy VIII and his sister Cleopatra II as rulers and resisted Antiochus' siege of Alexandria (169).

Antiochus withdrew, leaving Ptolemy VI at Memphis as a puppet king and keeping a garrison in Pelusium. But Ptolemy VI reconciled with his siblings, and the three ruled jointly from Alexandria. In 168 Antiochus invaded again, occupied Memphis (where he may have been crowned), sent a fleet to take Cyprus and advanced on Alexandria. At Eleusis, a suburb of Alexandria, he was met by the Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas, who handed him the Senate's ultimatum to leave Egypt; when Antiochus asked for time to consult, Popillius drew a circle around him in the sand and demanded an answer before he stepped out. Antiochus, knowing that Rome had just won at Pydna, complied and withdrew from Egypt and Cyprus.

The war marked the end of the Syrian Wars and the beginning of Roman protection of the Ptolemaic kingdom, which became increasingly dependent on Rome, whose Senate later arbitrated between the Ptolemaic brothers (163). For the Seleucids, the humiliation of Eleusis was followed by the crisis in Judaea and the Maccabean revolt. Sources include Polybius (books 28-29), Livy (44-45), Diodorus (30-31), Daniel (11.25-30) and Jerome's commentary, as well as demotic papyri, including the archive of Hor of Sebennytos, who claimed to have predicted Antiochus' departure.

scholarship: Grainger, The Syrian Wars (2010)
Ray, The Archive of Hor (1976)
Mørkholm, Antiochus IV of Syria (1966)

set.detail:
The Second Punic War (218-201), the Hannibalic War, was the greatest war of the Roman Republic and, Livy says, the most memorable ever waged. Its causes, analysed at length by Polybius, included Hamilcar's resentment after the First War, Rome's seizure of Sardinia (238/7), and Carthaginian expansion in Spain under the Barcids; the immediate pretext was Hannibal's siege of Saguntum (219), an ally of Rome south of the Ebro. Rome planned to fight in Spain and Africa, but Hannibal marched overland from Spain across the Alps into Italy in 218, arriving with 26,000 men.

The war passed through several phases. In 218-216 Hannibal won at the Ticinus, the Trebia, Trasimene and Cannae, where perhaps 50,000 Romans died, and won over Capua, much of Apulia, Samnium, Lucania and Bruttium. Fabius' strategy of attrition and Roman refusal to negotiate, the loyalty of the Latin colonies and central Italy, and the inexhaustible Roman manpower (more than 20 legions in the field in 212-211) prevented a Carthaginian victory. The war widened: Philip V allied with Hannibal (215), leading to the First Macedonian War; Syracuse defected (214) and was besieged and taken by Marcellus (213-212); in Spain the Scipio brothers fought from 218 until their deaths in 211. From 212 the tide turned: Rome retook Capua (211) despite Hannibal's march on Rome, recovered Tarentum (209) and destroyed Hasdrubal's relief army at the Metaurus (207). The young Scipio took New Carthage (209) and drove Carthage out of Spain at Baecula and Ilipa (208-206). In 204 he invaded Africa; Hannibal, recalled, was defeated at Zama (202).

The peace of 201 reduced Carthage to a dependent state, stripped of its fleet, its empire and its right to wage war. Rome gained Spain and became the dominant power in the western Mediterranean. The war devastated southern Italy, transformed Roman politics (with repeated consulships and long commands), and created a professional, experienced army and a governing class ready for eastern expansion. Polybius (books 3, 7-15) and Livy (books 21-30) are the main sources, with Appian, Plutarch, Dio and Zonaras. Modern scholarship continues to debate the war's causes, Hannibal's strategy and the reasons for Roman victory.

scholarship: Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage (2000)
Cornell, Rankov and Sabin (eds.), The Second Punic War: A Reappraisal (1996)
Hoyos (ed.), A Companion to the Punic Wars (2011)

set.detail:
The First Macedonian War (214-205) arose from Philip V's alliance with Hannibal (215), concluded after Cannae and revealed when Philip's envoy Xenophanes was captured by the Romans. Philip's aims, as shown by the treaty text preserved by Polybius, were limited to expelling Rome from the Illyrian protectorate, not invading Italy. In 214 he attacked Apollonia and Oricum with a fleet of 120 lembi but was surprised by the praetor Marcus Valerius Laevinus in a night attack and forced to burn his ships. In 213-212 he took Lissus and the Illyrian coast north of the protectorate by land.

Rome, fully occupied in Italy, sought allies: in 211 Laevinus concluded an alliance with the Aetolian League, whose terms gave the Aetolians the land and towns captured and the Romans the movable property, a treaty partly preserved on an inscription. Attalus I of Pergamon, Elis, Sparta, and the Illyrian chiefs Scerdilaidas and Pleuratus joined. The war was fought mainly by the Aetolians and Attalus, supported by a Roman fleet under Laevinus and then Publius Sulpicius Galba. Rome and its allies took Anticyra (210), Aegina (210, sold to Attalus for 30 talents), Oreus and Opus (208), enslaving their populations, which caused outrage in Greece. Philip defeated the Aetolians near Lamia (209) and recaptured Echinus (210), sacked Thermum again (206), and repelled Attalus, who withdrew in 208 to face Prusias.

With Rome sending no troops after 208, the Aetolians made a separate peace with Philip in 206. Rome then sent Publius Sempronius Tuditanus with 11,000 men, and the war was ended by the Peace of Phoenice (205), largely confirming the status quo, with Philip keeping Atintania. Neutral states (Egypt, Rhodes, Athens, Chios) had repeatedly tried to mediate. The war achieved Rome's objective of keeping Philip out of Italy at minimal cost, but left the Aetolians resentful and Philip free to expand east. Polybius (books 7-11, fragmentary) and Livy (books 24-29) are the main sources.

scholarship: Walbank, Philip V of Macedon (1940)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
Errington, Dawn of Empire (1971)

set.detail:
The Second Macedonian War (200-197) began with appeals to Rome from Attalus I, Rhodes and Athens after Philip V's aggressive campaigns in the Aegean, the Hellespont and Asia Minor (202-200), and the rumour of a pact between Philip and Antiochus III to divide the Ptolemaic empire. The comitia centuriata first rejected the declaration of war, then approved it after the consul Publius Sulpicius Galba's speech. Galba invaded Macedonia from Illyria in 199, winning a cavalry action at Ottolobus, while the Roman fleet and allies took Andros and raided Chalcis; Philip besieged Athens and ravaged Attica.

In 198 the new consul Titus Quinctius Flamininus forced Philip's position in the Aous gorge with the help of a local shepherd's guidance, advanced into Thessaly and Phocis, and won over the Achaean League at Sicyon, while his brother Lucius took Eretria. Peace negotiations at Nicaea failed when Flamininus, his command prorogued, demanded the evacuation of all Greece, including the 'fetters' (Demetrias, Chalcis, Corinth). In 197 Flamininus defeated Philip at Cynoscephalae in Thessaly; the Macedonian phalanx, caught on uneven ground, was destroyed by a flank attack. At the same time the Achaeans defeated the Macedonian garrison of Corinth and the Rhodians recovered their Peraea in Caria.

By the peace of 196 Philip withdrew from all Greek cities in Europe and Asia, surrendered his fleet except five ships and his royal galley, paid 1,000 talents and gave hostages, including his younger son Demetrius. Flamininus' Isthmian proclamation (196) declared the freedom of the Greeks, and the last Roman garrisons left in 194. The war established Rome as the arbiter of the Greek world and generated conflicts with the Aetolians, dissatisfied with their share, and Antiochus III, who expanded into Thrace. Modern historians debate the reasons for the war, from fear of Philip and Antiochus (Holleaux) to Roman desire for glory and booty (Harris) and the 'power-transition crisis' after the weakening of Egypt (Eckstein). Polybius (16-18) and Livy (31-33) are the main sources.

scholarship: Holleaux, Rome, la Grèce et les monarchies hellénistiques (1921)
Walbank, Philip V of Macedon (1940)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)

set.detail:
The Laconian War (195), or war against Nabis, was waged by Flamininus and a coalition of Greek states against Nabis, the last revolutionary king of Sparta (207-192). Nabis had freed helots, redistributed land, enrolled mercenaries and Cretan pirates and seized Argos from Philip V in 197 as the price of changing sides; he had been recognised by Rome as a friend. After the peace with Philip, the Achaeans, his bitter enemies, demanded that Rome liberate Argos, a test of the freedom proclaimed at the Isthmus.

In 195, after a Panhellenic congress at Corinth voted for war, Flamininus led a coalition army of about 50,000, including Roman legions, 10,000 Achaeans, Macedonians, Thessalians and Rhodian and Pergamene fleets under his brother Lucius, Eumenes II and the Rhodians. They took Gythium, Sparta's port, and besieged Sparta itself; the Romans broke into the city, but Nabis' men set fire to buildings and repelled them. Nabis then sued for peace. Flamininus, unwilling to prolong the war with Antiochus threatening, accepted terms: Nabis gave up Argos and the coastal towns of Laconia, which were placed under Achaean protection, surrendered his fleet, paid 500 talents and gave hostages, including his son Armenas.

The peace was unpopular with the Achaeans, who wanted Nabis destroyed, and Flamininus was accused of leaving Nabis in power as a counterweight to the Achaean League. Argos celebrated its liberation, and Flamininus presided over the Nemean Games. In 192, Nabis attempted to recover the coastal towns and was defeated by Philopoemen; he was then murdered by Aetolian 'allies' who wanted Sparta as a base for Antiochus, and Philopoemen brought Sparta into the Achaean League. Livy (34.22-41) is the main source, based on Polybius. The war illustrates the ambiguities of Roman 'freedom of the Greeks' and the importance of the Spartan question in Achaean-Roman relations, which ultimately led to the Achaean War of 146.

scholarship: Cartledge and Spawforth, Hellenistic and Roman Sparta (1989)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)

set.detail:
The Spanish revolt of 197-195 was the first great rising against Roman rule in Spain, which had been governed after Scipio's departure by private commanders and from 197 by two praetors. The cause, according to Livy, was the exactions of the Roman governors, the burden of tribute and requisitions and the arrival of permanent Roman administration. In 197 the Turdetani, led by the chieftain Culchas, who controlled 17 towns, and Luxinius, with Carmo and Baldo, rose in Hispania Ulterior, while the peoples of the east coast rose in Citerior. The praetor of Citerior, Gaius Sempronius Tuditanus, was defeated and died of his wounds.

In 196 the praetors Quintus Minucius Thermus (Citerior), who won at Turda, and Quintus Fabius Buteo (Ulterior) campaigned with some success. In 195 Rome sent the consul Marcus Porcius Cato with two legions, 15,000 allies and 20 ships to Citerior, while the praetor Publius Manlius took over in Ulterior. Cato landed at Emporiae, sent back his ships to force his men to fight, and defeated the Spanish army near Emporiae in a hard battle. He then marched through the province, crushing resistance, disarming the population and ordering the demolition of town walls on a single day. He tried to hire the Celtiberian mercenaries of the Turdetani, campaigned in the Ebro valley and the Celtiberian lands, and organised the silver and iron mines, from which Rome began to draw large revenues.

Cato returned to Rome and celebrated a triumph in 194, claiming to have taken more towns than he had spent days in Spain. The revolt continued in Ulterior until 194, when Scipio Nasica defeated the Lusitanians. The revolt was followed by almost continuous warfare in Spain for the next 60 years. Livy (33-34) and Cato's own speeches, preserved in fragments, are the main sources. Modern historians (Richardson, Astin) see the revolt as the moment when Rome realised it would have to maintain permanent armies in Spain to control it, and Cato's settlement as an important step in organising the provinces' finances.

scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)
Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)
Knapp, Aspects of the Roman Experience in Iberia (1977)

set.detail:
The Roman-Seleucid War, or Antiochene War (192-188), was the climax of the cold war between Rome and Antiochus III after the Second Macedonian War. The disputes concerned the freedom of the Greek cities of Asia Minor (Smyrna and Lampsacus appealed to Rome), Antiochus' presence in Thrace, where he rebuilt Lysimachia, and his reception of Hannibal (195). Negotiations at Lysimachia (196), Rome (193) and Ephesus failed. The Aetolians, embittered after Cynoscephalae, invited Antiochus to liberate Greece, and seized Demetrias in 192.

In autumn 192 Antiochus crossed to Greece with only 10,000 infantry, 500 cavalry and six elephants. He took Chalcis and won over Boeotia and Elis, but Philip V and the Achaeans sided with Rome. In 191 the consul Manius Acilius Glabrio defeated him at Thermopylae, thanks to Cato's outflanking march, and Antiochus fled to Asia. The war moved to the sea: the Roman fleet under Gaius Livius Salinator, with Eumenes II, defeated Polyxenidas off Corycus (191); the Rhodians lost a squadron at Panormus (190) but defeated Hannibal's Phoenician fleet off Side (the Eurymedon, 190), and Aemilius Regillus and the Rhodians destroyed Polyxenidas at Myonessus (190), opening the Hellespont. The consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio, with his brother Africanus as legate, crossed into Asia and defeated Antiochus at Magnesia ad Sipylum (190/189), with Domitius Ahenobarbus in effective command and Eumenes' cavalry decisive.

By the Treaty of Apamea (188), Antiochus lost all territory west of the Taurus, his fleet and elephants, and paid 15,000 talents. Eumenes and Rhodes received his Anatolian territories; Rome took nothing directly. The war made Rome the dominant power in the eastern Mediterranean and brought great wealth and Asian luxury to Rome, which Livy and later writers linked to moral decline (the triumph of Manlius Vulso). It also led to political conflicts in Rome, particularly the trials of the Scipios. Polybius (20-21) and Livy (35-38) are the main sources. Modern historians (Badian, Grainger) debate whether either side truly wanted war.

scholarship: Badian, Rome and Antiochus the Great: A Study in Cold War, CPh 54 (1959)
Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochos the Great (2002)
Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)

set.detail:
The Aetolian War (191-189) was the Roman war against the Aetolian League, which had invited Antiochus III to Greece in 192 and fought alongside him. After Antiochus' defeat at Thermopylae (191), the consul Manius Acilius Glabrio turned on the Aetolians, besieging and storming Heraclea Trachinia near Mount Oeta. The Aetolian envoys, led by Phaeneas, then agreed to entrust themselves 'to the faith of the Romans' (in fidem), believing it meant a negotiated alliance. When Glabrio demanded the surrender of their leaders and threatened to chain the envoys, they discovered that for Romans deditio in fidem meant unconditional surrender, an episode Polybius (20.9-10) uses to illustrate the clash of Greek and Roman diplomatic concepts.

The Aetolians resumed the war. Glabrio besieged Naupactus for two months until Flamininus intervened to arrange a truce. In 190 the Scipios granted a six-month armistice while they marched to Asia. Negotiations failed, and in 189 the consul Marcus Fulvius Nobilior besieged Ambracia, the former capital of Pyrrhus, which the Aetolians held. The defenders countermined the Roman mines and used a jar filled with feathers set alight and pumped with bellows to fill the Roman tunnel with smoke, a device Polybius describes (21.28). Athenian and Rhodian envoys mediated a peace, and Ambracia surrendered on terms; Fulvius took its art treasures, including the statues of the Muses, to Rome.

The peace of 189 required the Aetolians to pay 500 talents, give up the territories taken by Rome, and accept a clause to 'respect the empire and majesty of the Roman people' (maiestas clause), the first known appearance of this formula, which defined unequal relations. They also had to surrender hostages, and Cephallenia was separated from the League; Same revolted and was besieged for four months. The Aetolian League survived but was reduced to a minor power. The war illustrates the transformation of Roman relations with Greek states from partnership to dominance. Polybius (20-21) and Livy (36-38) are the main sources.

scholarship: Grainger, The League of the Aitolians (1999)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
Scholten, The Politics of Plunder (2000)

set.detail:
The Galatian War of 189 was the campaign of the consul Gnaeus Manlius Vulso against the Galatians, the Celtic peoples (Tolistobogii, Tectosages and Trocmi) who had settled in central Anatolia in the 270s and had served as mercenaries in Antiochus III's army at Magnesia. Vulso, who arrived after the decisive battle to take over the Roman army in Asia, launched the campaign without explicit senatorial authorisation, officially to punish the Galatians and to secure Asia Minor for Rome's ally Eumenes II, but also, according to his critics, for plunder and glory.

Vulso marched through Pisidia and Phrygia, extracting money from cities and rulers, and invaded Galatia with Attalus, Eumenes' brother. The Tolistobogii had retreated with their families to Mount Olympus, a fortified hilltop; the Romans, using a large force of light infantry and slingers, drove them from the heights with missiles, and the Galatians, armed with long swords and shields but without armour, suffered heavy losses. Livy (38.18-23), following Polybius, says 40,000 were killed or captured. Vulso then attacked the Tectosages and Trocmi on Mount Magaba near Ancyra, again defeating them. The wife of a Tolistobogian chief, Chiomara, raped by a centurion, had his head cut off at her ransom, an episode Polybius admired.

The Galatians sued for peace; the treaty of Apamea (188) required them to keep within their own territory and stop raiding. Vulso's return was marked by a Thracian ambush in which he lost much of the booty. In Rome, his triumph (187) was opposed by the commissioners of Apamea, who accused him of waging an unauthorised war, but he won the vote. Livy (39.6) says his army brought back Asian luxury: bronze couches, embroidered coverlets, female lute players and elaborate cooks, the 'origin of foreign luxury' in Rome. Modern historians see the campaign as an example of the growing independence of Roman commanders and the importance of booty in Roman warfare.

scholarship: Mitchell, Anatolia I (1993)
Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochos the Great (2002)

set.detail:
The First Celtiberian War (181-179) was the first large-scale Roman war against the Celtiberians, the Celtic-Iberian peoples of the central Meseta and the upper Ebro and Douro valleys (Arevaci, Belli, Titthi, Lusones and others), who served as mercenaries and raided the Roman provinces. In 182-181 the praetor of Citerior, Quintus Fulvius Flaccus, fought the Celtiberians and Carpetani, winning a battle near Aebura (181) and taking the town of Contrebia. In 180, while leaving his province with his veteran army, he was ambushed in the Manlian pass but fought his way through, vowing a temple to Fortuna Equestris.

The war was concluded by Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, praetor in Citerior (180-178), who campaigned with a large army, defeated the Celtiberians in several battles and took more than 100 towns, according to Livy, perhaps with exaggeration, including Complega. He founded Gracchurris (Alfaro) on the site of the native town of Ilurcis. His colleague in Ulterior, Lucius Postumius Albinus, campaigned against the Vaccaei and Lusitanians. Gracchus then made treaties with the Celtiberian peoples, which fixed their tribute (perhaps a twentieth of the harvest), their obligation to provide auxiliaries, and prohibited them from founding new fortified towns, although existing ones could be repaired.

The Gracchan treaties, based on mutual respect, brought peace to the region for about 25 years, until the Celtiberians of Segeda enlarged their walls in 154, leading to the Second Celtiberian War. Gracchus' reputation for fairness among the Celtiberians lasted a generation; his son Tiberius, as quaestor at Numantia in 137, was able to negotiate the release of Mancinus' army because of it. Livy (40.30-50) and Appian (Iberica 42-43) are the main sources. Modern historians (Richardson) see the war and its settlement as the beginning of a more systematic Roman administration in Spain, with regular tribute and military obligations, and the Gracchan treaties as an example of Roman diplomatic flexibility.

scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)
Curchin, Roman Spain: Conquest and Assimilation (1991)
Lorrio, Los Celtíberos (1997)

set.detail:
The Sardinian War of 177-176 was the last major revolt against Roman rule in Sardinia, which had been a Roman province since 227. The Ilienses (or Iolaei) and Balari, peoples of the mountainous interior who had never been fully subdued and were remembered as descendants of Trojans and other migrants, attacked the Roman province in 178 with help from the Corsicans. The praetor of Sardinia was unable to contain them, and the Senate sent the consul Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, who had already distinguished himself in Spain, with two legions, 1,200 cavalry and allied troops.

In 177 Gracchus defeated the Sardinians in a battle in which, according to Livy, 12,000 were killed; in 176, with his command prorogued, he won another battle, killing 15,000 and receiving the surrender of all of Sardinia. He imposed double tribute on the rebellious peoples and took hostages. So many Sardinians were enslaved that 'Sardi venales' ('Sardinians for sale', meaning cheap goods) became a proverbial expression, according to Festus and Aurelius Victor. Gracchus celebrated a triumph in 175 and dedicated in the temple of Mater Matuta a bronze tablet in the shape of Sardinia, with pictures of the battles and an inscription recording that 80,000 enemies were killed or captured.

The war broke the resistance of the interior peoples for several decades, although Sardinia remained a difficult province, with further campaigns recorded in the 120s (the triumph of Lucius Aurelius Orestes in 122) and the 110s (Marcus Caecilius Metellus, 111). Sardinia's main importance to Rome was as a source of grain. The rebellious peoples of the interior, called by the Romans the Barbaria (modern Barbagia), retained their way of life into the imperial period. Livy (41.6-28) is the main source. Modern historians (Dyson, Rowland) see the war and its harsh settlement as typical of Roman treatment of 'barbarian' peoples in contrast to the more moderate treatment of the Greek East, and the tablet as an early example of Roman cartographic display.

scholarship: Dyson and Rowland, Archaeology and History in Sardinia from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages (2007)
Meloni, La Sardegna romana (1975)

set.detail:
The Third Macedonian War (171-168) ended the Antigonid monarchy. Perseus, who succeeded Philip V in 179, renewed the friendship with Rome but sought to restore Macedonian prestige in Greece through popular measures, alliances (marrying Laodice, daughter of Seleucus IV, and giving his sister to Prusias II) and interventions in Thessaly, Aetolia and Boeotia. Eumenes II denounced him before the Senate in 172, and the attack on Eumenes at Delphi was blamed on him. Rome, after lulling Perseus with negotiations led by Quintus Marcius Philippus, declared war in 171.

The first years went badly for Rome. In 171 Perseus defeated the cavalry of the consul Publius Licinius Crassus at Callinicus but failed to exploit his victory, offering peace on the terms of 196. Roman commanders plundered Greek allies (Haliartus, Chalcis, Abdera, Coronea), which provoked complaints and trials. In 170 the consul Aulus Hostilius Mancinus achieved little, and Appius Claudius Cento was defeated in Illyria near Uscana. In 169 the consul Quintus Marcius Philippus crossed into Pieria via difficult mountain passes, but stalled against Perseus' line on the Elpeus. Perseus enlisted Genthius of Illyria but alienated him and Bastarnian mercenaries through his avarice.

In 168 Lucius Aemilius Paullus took command, restored discipline, outflanked the Elpeus line via Pythium and defeated Perseus at Pydna (22 June 168). Genthius was crushed by Lucius Anicius in thirty days. Perseus surrendered at Samothrace and was paraded in Paullus' triumph (167). The monarchy was abolished; Macedonia was divided into four republics and Illyria into three; 70 towns of Epirus were sacked and 150,000 people enslaved; 1,000 Achaeans, including Polybius, were deported; Rhodes was punished. Polybius saw 168 as the end of the 53 years in which Rome conquered the world. Livy (42-45) is the main source; Polybius (27-30) survives in fragments.

scholarship: Burton, Rome and the Third Macedonian War (2017)
Gruen, Class Conflict and the Third Macedonian War, AJAH 1 (1976)
Hammond and Walbank, A History of Macedonia III (1988)

set.detail:
The Dalmatian War (156-155) was Rome's first war against the Dalmatae, an Illyrian people of the Adriatic hinterland north of the Neretva, centred on Delminium (near Tomislavgrad in modern Bosnia). After the fall of the Illyrian kingdom of Genthius (168), the Dalmatae had broken away and attacked Roman allies: the Greek city of Issa and its colonies on the mainland (Tragurium and Epetium), and the Daorsi, an Illyrian people who were allies of Rome. A Roman embassy under Gaius Fannius was insulted, according to Polybius (32.13), who says the Dalmatae refused to listen and denied hospitality to the envoys.

The Senate decided on war, partly, Polybius says, because the Romans thought their soldiers had become soft after twelve years without war in the East, and wanted to keep them in training. In 156 the consul Gaius Marcius Figulus invaded Dalmatia but was surprised in camp and forced to retreat to the Neretva; he later besieged Delminium without success. In 155 the consul Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum took over and captured Delminium, which the Romans set on fire by throwing incendiary stakes over the walls. He celebrated a triumph over the Dalmatae.

The war was a limited punitive campaign rather than a conquest: the Dalmatae were not annexed and remained a troublesome independent people, requiring further campaigns in 119 (Lucius Caecilius Metellus Dalmaticus), 78-76, under Caesar and Octavian (34-33), and in the great Illyrian revolt of AD 6-9. The war illustrates the Roman practice of using limited wars to defend allies and maintain prestige, and Polybius' observation about the desire to keep the army in training has been used in debates about Roman imperialism (Harris). The main sources are Polybius (32.13), Appian (Illyrica 11) and the Livian Periochae (47).

scholarship: Wilkes, Dalmatia (1969)
Dzino, Illyricum in Roman Politics (2010)
Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)

set.detail:
The Second Celtiberian War (154-151) broke the peace established by Tiberius Gracchus' treaties in 179. In 154 the Belli of Segeda began to enlarge the circuit of their walls and to force neighbouring peoples to settle within them; Rome considered this a breach of the treaty clause prohibiting new fortified towns, and demanded that the work stop and that tribute and auxiliaries be provided. The Segedans refused, claiming that the treaty only prohibited founding new towns, not fortifying existing ones. Rome sent the consul Quintus Fulvius Nobilior with nearly 30,000 men; to allow him to arrive in time for the campaign, the consuls took office on 1 January 153 instead of 15 March, a change that became permanent.

The Segedans fled to the Arevaci of Numantia, who chose the Segedan Carus as their leader. On the feast of the Vulcanalia (23 August) 153, Carus ambushed Nobilior's army, killing 6,000 Romans, a date thereafter considered unlucky. Nobilior advanced to Numantia with elephants provided by Masinissa, but when an elephant was struck by a stone and panicked, the others stampeded through the Roman lines, and the Numantines routed the Romans. The winter was disastrous. In 152 the consul Marcus Claudius Marcellus, consul for the third time, took Ocilis and Nertobriga with moderation and negotiated with the Celtiberians; when the Senate rejected his peace, he concluded it anyway before his successor arrived, on the basis of the Gracchan treaties and a payment of 600 talents.

In Rome, the fear of the Celtiberian war led to a levy crisis in 151, when young men refused to serve and tribunes imprisoned the consuls; the young Scipio Aemilianus volunteered and others followed. Lucius Licinius Lucullus, consul in 151, found peace already concluded and attacked the Vaccaei without authorisation, massacring the people of Cauca and failing at Intercatia and Pallantia. Polybius (35.1-5) describes the 'fiery war' and its effect on Roman morale. Appian (Iberica 44-55) is the main narrative source. The war left the Arevaci at peace with Rome until 143.

scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)
Simon, Roms Kriege in Spanien (1962)
Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)

set.detail:
The Lusitanian War (155-139) was a long war against the Lusitanians, a people of the western Iberian Peninsula between the Tagus and the Douro (central Portugal and western Spain), who raided the Roman province of Hispania Ulterior and its allies. In 155 the Lusitanians under Punicus defeated the praetors Manius Manilius and Lucius Calpurnius Piso; in 153 Punicus' successor Caesarus defeated the praetor Lucius Mummius. In 151-150 the praetor Servius Sulpicius Galba and the consul Lucius Licinius Lucullus ravaged Lusitania; in 150 Galba, offering land to the Lusitanians, massacred those who laid down their arms, an act that provoked outrage and the trial of 149.

In 147 Viriathus, a survivor of the massacre, took command and began an eight-year campaign of guerrilla warfare, defeating the praetor Gaius Vetilius at Tribola (147), Gaius Plautius (146), Claudius Unimanus and Gaius Nigidius (145). Quintus Fabius Maximus Aemilianus (145-144) checked him, but Viriathus incited the Celtiberians to rise (143), beginning the Numantine War. In 141-140, Quintus Fabius Maximus Servilianus won some successes but was trapped by Viriathus near Erisane; Viriathus spared the army in exchange for a treaty that recognised him as a friend of the Roman people, ratified in Rome.

In 140/139 Servilianus' brother Quintus Servilius Caepio, with the Senate's connivance, broke the treaty and bribed three of Viriathus' companions to murder him. His successor Tautalus surrendered, and the Lusitanians were settled at Valentia (138) by Decimus Junius Brutus, who campaigned north to Gallaecia (137-136), crossing the Douro and the Limia (Lethe). The war was marked by Roman bad faith and brutality and by the military skill of Viriathus. Appian (Iberica 56-75), based on Polybius and Posidonius, and Diodorus (33) are the main sources. Modern historians debate the social character of Lusitanian resistance (poverty driving raids, as Appian suggests) and the role of Viriathus as a national hero in Portuguese tradition.

scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)
Pastor Muñoz, Viriato: la lucha por la libertad (2000)
Alarcão, Roman Portugal (1988)

set.detail:
The Fourth Macedonian War (150-148) was the revolt of Andriscus, a man of humble origin from Adramyttium in Mysia who claimed to be Philip, a son of Perseus who had died in Italy. Andriscus first sought support from Demetrius I of Syria, who handed him over to Rome; he escaped from custody in Italy, raised support among the Thracians, and in 149 invaded Macedonia, defeated the forces of the merides and proclaimed himself king as Philip VI. The four republics established in 167, weak and divided, collapsed quickly, and Andriscus reunited Macedonia, revealing the strength of Macedonian monarchist sentiment.

Andriscus invaded Thessaly in 149. Rome, occupied with Carthage and Spain, sent the praetor Publius Juventius Thalna with a single legion, which was destroyed, Juventius himself being killed, the only time in this period that a Roman army was destroyed in the Greek East. Scipio Nasica Corculum had earlier helped the Thessalians with Achaean troops. In 148 Rome sent the praetor Quintus Caecilius Metellus with two legions, supported by the fleet of Attalus II of Pergamon. Metellus defeated Andriscus near Pydna, the site of Aemilius Paullus' victory twenty years earlier. Andriscus fled to Thrace, where a Thracian chief, Byzes, handed him over; he was led in Metellus' triumph (146) and executed.

In 148 or 146 Rome made Macedonia a permanent province, abandoning the system of four republics, with a governor responsible for defending the northern frontier and supervising Greece; the Via Egnatia was built soon afterwards. Further pretenders appeared in 143 and 142 (a pseudo-Alexander and a pseudo-Philip), easily suppressed. The war marked the shift from indirect hegemony to direct rule in the Greek East, closely connected with the Achaean War (146). The sources are fragmentary: the Livian Periochae (49-50), Diodorus (32), Florus, Velleius, Zonaras and Polybius (36.10, 36.17), who expressed astonishment that such a man could succeed.

scholarship: Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)
Morgan, Metellus Macedonicus and the Province Macedonia, Historia 18 (1969)
Hammond and Walbank, A History of Macedonia III (1988)

set.detail:
The Third Punic War (149-146) resulted in the destruction of Carthage. After 201, Carthage had recovered economically, paying off its indemnity and offering to pay it early in 191. Masinissa, protected by the vague clause of the treaty of 201 allowing him to recover his ancestral lands, seized Carthaginian territory, notably the Emporia (161) and the Great Plains (c. 152), with Roman acquiescence. Cato, after an embassy in 153, demanded the destruction of Carthage, opposed by Scipio Nasica Corculum. In 150 Carthage, provoked, fought Masinissa and was defeated near Oroscopa; this breach of the treaty gave Rome its pretext.

In 149 Rome declared war; Utica surrendered to Rome, and the consuls Manius Manilius and Lucius Marcius Censorinus crossed with 80,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry. Carthage surrendered by deditio, handed over 300 hostages and 200,000 sets of armour and 2,000 catapults, but when the consuls demanded that the city be abandoned and rebuilt inland, the Carthaginians resisted. The siege lasted three years: the consuls of 149 and 148 failed; Manilius was beaten at Nepheris, where the military tribune Scipio Aemilianus distinguished himself. In 147 the people elected Aemilianus consul, though below the legal age. He restored discipline, took the suburb of Megara, cut the city off by a siege wall across the isthmus and a mole across the harbour, defeated the Carthaginian fleet that broke out through a new channel, and destroyed the field army at Nepheris. In spring 146 he stormed the city; after six days of street fighting, 50,000 survivors surrendered and were enslaved, and the city was razed.

Carthaginian territory became the province of Africa, governed from Utica. Polybius, an eyewitness, saw Scipio weep over Carthage, quoting Homer. The war is a classic case in debates on Roman imperialism: ancient writers (Sallust, Posidonius) saw the removal of the 'fear of the enemy' (metus hostilis) as the start of Roman moral decline. Appian (Punica 67-135), based on Polybius, is the main source.

scholarship: Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Lancel, Carthage (1995)
Le Bohec, Histoire militaire des guerres puniques (1996)
Miles, Carthage Must Be Destroyed (2010)

set.detail:
The Achaean War (146) ended the independence of the Achaean League and of Greece. Its origins lay in the long dispute over Sparta, which had been forced into the Achaean League in 192 and repeatedly appealed to Rome against Achaean interference, and in the return in 150 of the Achaean exiles deported in 167, among whom were bitter enemies of Rome. In 149-148 Sparta, encouraged by Roman non-intervention, seceded from the League; the Achaean general Damocritus and then Diaeus attacked it. In 147 the Roman envoy Lucius Aurelius Orestes announced at Corinth that Sparta, Corinth, Argos, Heraclea and Orchomenus should be detached from the League. Riots broke out, and Spartans and perhaps Roman envoys were insulted.

The radical leaders Critolaus and Diaeus led the League to war in 146, appealing to the people with debt relief and, in Diaeus' case, arming 12,000 slaves. Critolaus marched north against Heraclea in Thessaly but was defeated by Quintus Caecilius Metellus at Scarpheia in Locris and disappeared. Metellus advanced towards the Isthmus. The consul Lucius Mummius then took command and defeated Diaeus at Leucopetra on the Isthmus. Diaeus killed his wife and himself. Mummius sacked Corinth, killing the men, enslaving the women and children and razing the city on the Senate's orders.

The ten senatorial commissioners dissolved the Achaean League and other leagues (later partly restored), abolished democracies, set up property-based oligarchies, and imposed tribute on some cities. Greece was placed under the supervision of the governor of Macedonia, although it was not formally organised as the province of Achaea until 27. Polybius, who helped with the settlement, regarded the year 146 as the end of the period covered by his history and blamed the 'madness' of the Achaean leaders and the masses. Pausanias (7.11-16) is the main narrative source, with Polybius (38-39) in fragments. Modern historians (Gruen, Kallet-Marx) debate whether Rome deliberately sought to break up the League or reacted to Achaean provocations, and stress the social dimension of the Achaean rising.

scholarship: Gruen, The Origins of the Achaean War, JHS 96 (1976)
Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)

set.detail:
The Numantine War (143-133) was the final phase of the Celtiberian wars, centred on Numantia, the main town of the Arevaci, on a hill at the confluence of the Douro and Merdancho near modern Soria. In 143, encouraged by Viriathus, the Arevaci rose again. The consul Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus (143-142) subdued much of Celtiberia but not Numantia and Termantia. His successor Quintus Pompeius (141-140) suffered repeated defeats at Numantia and made a secret peace with the Numantines, which he then denied; the Senate repudiated it (139). Marcus Popillius Laenas (139-138) was defeated.

In 137 the consul Gaius Hostilius Mancinus, panicked by a false rumour, was surrounded with 20,000 men by 4,000 Numantines; his quaestor Tiberius Gracchus negotiated a treaty that saved the army. The Senate repudiated the treaty and handed Mancinus, naked and bound, to the Numantines, who refused him (136). Marcus Aemilius Lepidus Porcina (137-136) attacked the Vaccaei without authorisation and failed at Pallantia; Lucius Furius Philus and Quintus Calpurnius Piso (136-135) achieved nothing. The war caused a crisis of recruitment in Rome, with tribunes imprisoning consuls in 138.

In 134 the people elected Scipio Aemilianus consul in breach of the law prohibiting second consulships. Scipio restored discipline in the demoralised army, ravaged the land of the Vaccaei, and surrounded Numantia with a circumvallation of nine kilometres, with seven camps, towers and a barrier across the Douro, with 60,000 men against perhaps 8,000 defenders. After eight months of famine and cannibalism, Numantia surrendered in 133; many inhabitants killed themselves, the rest were sold, and the town was razed. Scipio took the name Numantinus. The siege works excavated by Adolf Schulten are among the best preserved Roman camps of the Republic. The war's failures and its cost in manpower were part of the background to Tiberius Gracchus' reforms. Appian (Iberica 76-98), based on Polybius' monograph, is the main source.

scholarship: Schulten, Numantia I-IV (1914-1931)
Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Dobson, The Army of the Roman Republic: Polybius and the Camps at Numantia (2008)

set.detail:
The First Servile War (135-132) was the largest slave revolt in the ancient world before Spartacus. It broke out in Sicily, where wealthy Sicilian and Roman landowners had acquired large numbers of slaves, many recently enslaved in Rome's eastern wars, to work vast estates and herds; according to Diodorus (following Posidonius), the masters treated them brutally, branding, chaining and underfeeding them, and allowing herdsmen to rob travellers for their food. The revolt began at Enna, where the slaves of Damophilus, led by Eunus, a Syrian slave from Apamea who claimed prophetic powers and breathed fire, killed their masters and seized the town. Eunus took the royal name Antiochus, formed a council and minted coins.

A second revolt led by Cleon, a Cilician herdsman, broke out near Agrigentum; he joined Eunus as his general. The rebels, said to have numbered from 70,000 to 200,000, defeated several Roman praetors (Lucius Hypsaeus among them) and took Tauromenium and much of the island. Rome, occupied with Numantia, responded slowly. Revolts inspired by the Sicilian example broke out at Minturnae, Sinuessa, in Attica (Laurion mines) and on Delos. In 134 the consul Gaius Fulvius Flaccus and in 133 Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi fought the rebels, Piso besieging Enna.

In 132 the consul Publius Rupilius besieged and starved Tauromenium, where the defenders resorted to cannibalism, and took it by treachery; he then took Enna, where Cleon died fighting. Eunus fled, was captured and died in prison at Morgantina. Over 20,000 slaves were crucified, according to Orosius. Rupilius, with ten commissioners, drew up the lex Rupilia regulating the administration of Sicily. The war was part of the social crisis of the period: Tiberius Gracchus' reforms of 133 aimed partly to address the replacement of free peasants by slaves. Diodorus (34/35.2), preserved in Byzantine excerpts, is the main source. Modern historians (Bradley, Shaw, Urbainczyk) debate whether the revolt aimed at a new kingdom on a Hellenistic model or at ending slavery.

scholarship: Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World (1989)
Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)
Morton, Eunus: The Cowardly King, CQ 63 (2013)

set.detail:
The revolt of Aristonicus (133-129) followed the death of Attalus III of Pergamon in 133, who bequeathed his kingdom to the Roman people, except the city of Pergamon and other Greek cities, which he declared free. Aristonicus, claiming to be an illegitimate son of Eumenes II, contested the will and took the royal name Eumenes III, minting coins with that name. He first won support in coastal cities, taking Leucae, Phocaea and Colophon, but was defeated off Cyme by the Ephesian fleet. He then turned inland, appealing to slaves and the poor, whom he called 'Heliopolitae' (citizens of the City of the Sun), an idea associated with the utopian fiction of Iambulus and the Stoic Blossius of Cumae, Tiberius Gracchus' adviser, who joined him.

Rome was slow to respond, sending a commission of five senators in 132. In 131 the consul Publius Licinius Crassus Dives Mucianus, pontifex maximus and jurist, arrived with an army, supported by the kings of Bithynia (Nicomedes II), Cappadocia (Ariarathes V, killed in the war), Pontus (Mithridates V) and Paphlagonia. In 130 Crassus was defeated near Leucae and captured; he provoked a Thracian guard into killing him to avoid capture. The consul Marcus Perperna then defeated Aristonicus, besieged him at Stratonicea on the Caicus, and captured him; Aristonicus was taken to Rome and strangled in prison, and Perperna died at Pergamon. Manius Aquillius, consul in 129, completed the pacification, reportedly poisoning the wells of rebel towns.

With ten commissioners, Aquillius organised the province of Asia (129-126), giving Greater Phrygia to Mithridates V (later revoked) and Lycaonia to Cappadocia; he built roads, some milestones of which survive. The province's wealth, its tax-farming by Roman publicani under Gaius Gracchus' law (123), and Roman exploitation would contribute to the massacre of Romans in 88 under Mithridates VI. The revolt has been interpreted as a social revolution or a dynastic war; modern historians (Gruen, Kallet-Marx) emphasise its dynastic character. Sources are scattered: Strabo, Justin, the Livian Periochae, Florus, Orosius and inscriptions.

scholarship: Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)
Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
